p.src: Overview: A single electron spin is the first genuinely quantum bit. It may be prepared relative to any spatial direction, yet a fixed detector returns only two outcomes. We let the classical magnetic picture fail, then construct the complex vector space, probability rule, and matrix language needed to describe what the experiment actually does.

ja: 概観: 単一の電子スピンは、最初の真に量子力学的なビットである。それは任意の空間方向に対して準備されうるが、固定された検出器は二つの結果しか返さない。ここでは古典的な磁石の描像をいったん放棄し、実験が実際に行っていることを記述するために必要な複素ベクトル空間、確率規則、そして行列の言葉を構成する。

p.src: One Spin and Two Meanings of Vector

u.src: One Spin and Two Meanings of Vector
en: One Spin and Two Meanings of Vector

p.src: A classical bit has two possible states and nothing between them. We may call them $0$ and $1$, heads and tails, or up and down; the names are labels for two distinct points in a classical state space. A quantum bit also yields two alternatives when measured in a fixed way, but it cannot be described by only two state-space points. The simplest example is the spin of an electron.

p.src: There are two different notions of vector in this example, and confusing them makes everything that follows unnecessarily mysterious. First there is an ordinary spatial vector: an arrow in three-dimensional space with a magnitude and a direction. The electron has a magnetic moment that behaves, for the present purpose, like a tiny magnet. Its magnitude is fixed, while a spatial direction can be assigned to it in a preparation procedure.

p.src: The second object is an abstract vector in a complex vector space. This state vector will describe the quantum state. It is not simply the magnetic arrow written in another notation. zh: 第二种对象是复矢量空间中的抽象矢量。这个态矢量将描述量子态。它并不只是用另一种记号写出的磁箭头。空间方向与态矢量之间的关系是真实而重要的，但它并不是两个对象的同一性。我们将逐步获得这种关系。

p.src: Begin deliberately with a classical story. Put a tiny magnet in a strong external magnetic field. Unless it is already aligned, it precesses about the field. As it radiates energy, the precession damps and the magnet settles into its lowest-energy orientation. By choosing the direction of the applied field, waiting for this relaxation, and then removing the field, we seem able to prepare the magnetic moment in any desired direction.

As it radiates energy, the precession damps and the magnet settles into its lowest-energy orientation. ja: まず意図的に古典的な物語から始めよう。小さな磁石を強い外部磁場の中に置く。すでに整列していない限り、それは磁場のまわりで歳差運動をする。エネルギーを放射するにつれて歳差運動は減衰し、磁石は最低エネルギーの向きに落ち着く。印加磁場の向きを選び、この緩和を待ち、その後磁場を取り除くことによって、磁気モーメントを任意の望む向きに準備できるように思われる。
zh: 有意从一个经典故事开始。将一个小磁体放入强外磁场中。除非它已经对齐，否则它会绕磁场进动。当它辐射能量时，进动逐渐阻尼，磁体最终稳定到其最低能量的取向。通过选择所施加磁场的方向、等待这种弛豫、然后撤去磁场，我们似乎能够将磁矩制备到任意期望的方向。

p.src: The same apparatus suggests a method of detection. Turn on a field in a chosen direction and observe the radiation produced while the little magnet settles. A classical magnet aligned with the field should emit no energy. One initially opposed to the field should emit the maximum amount, and an intermediate angle should produce an intermediate amount. In that picture the radiated energy varies continuously with the angle.

zh: 同一套装置提示了一种探测方法。在选定方向上开启磁场，并观察小磁体稳定过程中产生的辐射。与磁场对齐的经典磁体应当不发射能量。最初与磁场反向的磁体应当发射最大能量，而中间角度应当产生中间大小的能量。在那幅图像中，辐射能量随角度连续变化。

p.src:
The direction used in preparation has not become irrelevant. It controls the probabilities of the two answers. Prepare the electron up relative to the detector and the up result occurs with certainty. Prepare it down and the transition occurs with certainty. Prepare it horizontally and a vertical detector returns the two answers equally often: $P(\text{up})=\frac12,
  \qquad
  P(\text{down})=\frac12.$ Thus a continuously variable family of preparations leads to a two-valued measurement whose statistics vary continuously.

After the first measurement, repeating the same measurement on that electron gives the same result; the measurement has prepared it relative to that detector. Waiting for a radiative transition is itself one possible preparation procedure.

The required state space is linear: its elements can be added and multiplied by scalars. Its scalars are complex numbers. Write $z=a+ib,

  i^2=-1,

  &=(a-ib)(a+ib) \notag\\
  &=a^2+b^2.
  \end{aligned}$ This simple cancellation is the algebraic seed of the probability rule.

p.src:
Real two-dimensional vectors make the geometry visible. The matrices $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ respectively stretch every direction uniformly, stretch only the $y$-component, and stretch only the $x$-component. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ interchanges the components and reflects the plane across $x=y$. Meanwhile, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix}v_x\\v_y\end{pmatrix}
  =
  \begin{pmatrix}v_y\\-v_x\end{pmatrix}$ rotates vectors through a clockwise quarter-turn in the convention used at the board. A shear supplies another linear example, although its matrix is left as practice. The essential restriction is linearity: not every imaginable transformation of the plane is represented by a matrix.

    r&4+i\\

  \end{pmatrix},
